children: GOOD = BAD? AN AUGUST JOBS REPORT DEEP DIVE
The August employment report blasted past expectations. Great news, right?
The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs last month, nearly three times the 56,000 consensus.
On top of that, June and July payrolls were upwardly revised by 11,000 and 44,000, respectively, and with July now showing 21,000 job adds compared with the originally stated 23,000 loss.
This marks the fifth upside surprise in the past 12 months, and the fourth reading to print above the 100,000 level over the same period.

Drilling below the headline, an 86,000 increase in the often lower-wage services sector was responsible for 67.7% of the 127,000 private-sector job additions, a smaller-than-usual share. Goods-producing and construction sectors added 41,000 and 22,000 jobs, respectively. The manufacturing sector added 16,000 workers, versus the 5,000 expected. Government payrolls increased by 35,000.
While all of that is hunky-dory, the odds of a near-term rate hike from Warsh & Co have increased.
Financial markets are currently baking in 58.2% likelihood of a rate hike at the conclusion of the Fed's September meeting, up from 49.4% yesterday, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Is this a case of good news is bad news?
Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, thinks so.

"Although it’s not a given that the Fed will raise rates on September 16, especially given the optics of a national election less than 2 months after the meeting, there are plenty of reasons to raise interest rates (to fight inflation) and less reasons to keep rates unchanged (to support the labor market)," Zaccarelli writes.

The report also gave markets their first glimpse of August inflation, showing average hourly wages accelerating slightly to 0.2% on a monthly basis, as expected. Year-on-year, wage growth cooled a bit, to 3.1% from 3.2%. But analysts predicted a slightly larger drop, to an even 3.0%.

While annual wage growth is stronger than the most recent core CPI reading of 2.5%, it's cooler than 3.4% headline CPI. That means real wage growth is in negative territory, if you factor in food and energy prices. That bodes ill for consumers, who carry about 70% of the U.S. economy on their shoulders.

"The labor market remains a source of muted inflation pressure," writes Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "The low quits rate is enabling employers to stand their ground in wage negotiations."
Elsewhere in the report, the uptick in the labor market participation rate — to 61.6% from 61.4% — is a step in the right direction.
Especially considering the unemployment rate held firm at a low 4.1%.
Typically, increasing participation puts upward pressure on the jobless rate; when workers are on the sidelines, they're not considered unemployed.
Despite the participation uptick, it's still very low by historical standards, lest we get too excited.

The average unemployment duration increased to 26.1 weeks from July's 23.7. That metric has been zig-zagging higher for about two years, and corresponds with the general downward trend of jobs confidence reflected in consumer survey data.

Broken down by race and ethnicity, joblessness among White workers ticked a shade higher, to 3.7% from 3.6%, still well below the national average. Unemployment among those who identify as Hispanic increased to 4.8%, while Asian unemployment dipped to 3.3%. The jobless rate among Black workers decreased to an even 6.0%, the lowest level in a year and a half.
Taken together, the White/Black jobless gap dropped to 2.3 pps, the narrowest it's been since October 2024.
"Unemployment among Black workers often serves as a bellwether of trends in the broader labor market," notes Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Commercial Bank.
